title: Colossal Cretaceous Octopus Dwarfed Even Giant Marine Reptiles
summary: Long before sailors whispered about the kraken, a real leviathan lurked in the Cretaceous seas. A new study of fossil jaws suggests that a colossal octopus, stretching up to 63 feet (19 meters) from head to arm tip, dominated the oceans while dinosaurs roamed the land. That's roughly the length of a school bus—and possibly the largest invertebrate in Earth's history. The problem with studying ancient octopuses is that their soft bodies rarely fossilize. But these creatures had a hard, beak-like jaw made of chitin, a durable material that can survive millions of years. Paleontologist Yasuhiro Iba of Hokkaido University and his team examined 15 such jaws from Japan and Vancouver Island, dating to the Late Cretaceous (66–100 million years ago). Some fossils were too fragile to extract, so the team used digital fossil mining: they ground down rock layers, photographed each slice, and used AI to reconstruct detailed 3-D models. The 27 specimens, once thought to represent five species, were narrowed to just two: the smaller Nanaimoteuthis jeletzkyi and the enormous N. haggarti. The largest lower jaw of N. haggarti could cradle a grapefruit and was about 50 percent larger than that of today's giant squid, which can reach 39 feet. Iba estimates the ancient octopus spanned 23 to 63 feet, dwarfing even the giant marine reptiles of its time, such as mosasaurs and long-necked plesiosaurs. The jaws bore scratches and wear, indicating the octopus was a powerful predator that crunched shells and bones—likely competing with those reptiles for a top spot in the food chain. These behemoths were early finned octopuses, relatives of today's deep-sea dumbo octopus, but on a scale almost unimaginable. The finding, published April 23 in Science, rewrites our picture of ancient ocean ecosystems. It shows that while dinosaurs thundered on land, an equally spectacular drama unfolded beneath the waves—with an octopus the size of a bus as a leading character.
why_it_matters: This discovery reveals that the age of giants was not just on land—it thrived in the seas too, challenging our ideas about what kinds of animals can grow to enormous sizes. It also shows how technology like digital fossil mining can unlock the secrets of ancient soft-bodied creatures that would otherwise be lost forever.

background_read: The Cretaceous Period (145–66 million years ago) was dominated by dinosaurs on land and giant marine reptiles like mosasaurs and plesiosaurs in the oceans. Mosasaurs could reach lengths of over 50 feet, yet this newly described octopus may have been even larger.

Fossils of ancient octopuses are extremely rare because they lack bones; only the chitinous beak sometimes survives. The giant squid (Architeuthis), the largest living invertebrate, can grow to about 39 feet, but the beak of N. haggarti was 50% bigger.

Yasuhiro Iba (a paleontologist at Hokkaido University in Sapporo, Japan) used a technique called digital fossil mining, where rock is ground away layer by layer and photographs are fed to AI to build a 3D model.
The dumbo octopus (Grimpoteuthis), a modern deep-sea relative, swims using large fins that look like ears, giving a hint of what these ancient creatures might have resembled.
Legends of the kraken, a mythical sea monster from Scandinavian folklore that could drag down ships, might have been inspired by encounters with giant cephalopods.

perspectives.description: Researchers are thrilled to finally have evidence of a giant predatory octopus from the Cretaceous. This fills a gap in the food web, showing that invertebrates could compete with large marine reptiles as apex predators. It’s a reminder that the age of dinosaurs had equally impressive creatures in the sea.

Critics caution that estimating total body length from just the jaw can lead to overestimates. Soft tissues like the mantle and arms vary widely in proportion among octopus species, so a 50% larger jaw might not mean a 50% longer animal. Without more fossils, the upper bound of 63 feet remains speculative.

Because soft-bodied animals rarely fossilize, our view of ancient life is skewed toward shelled and bony organisms. The discovery underscores how much we might be missing—giant octopuses and other invertebrates may have been common but left almost no trace. This evolutionary blind spot challenges scientists to develop new methods.

The success of digital fossil mining and AI reconstruction opens doors for examining other fragile specimens. Future expeditions might target Cretaceous rock formations that preserve chitin, or use similar techniques on existing museum collections. Finding a more complete beak or even an ink sac impression could refine size estimates and reveal more about the octopus's ecology.
